content: decolonial.ist Knowledge Base Tour Contribute FAQ contact@decolonial.ist DECOLONIAL.IST is a knowledge base of Russian colonialism, built on the experience of the peoples who survived it and are living through it still. The project treats the Tsardom of Muscovy, the Russian Empire, the USSR and the Russian Federation as one empire, a single actor of colonial policy. Documented campaigns from the 16th century to the present demonstrate the recurrence of the methods of colonization. The project studies the empire the way military analysts study an adversary: through its recurring tactics, techniques and procedures, in order to predict its actions and prepare countermeasures. The primary sources of the knowledge base are collected in an open archive: the testimony of survivors and of the colonizers themselves, the empire's laws and decrees, court rulings, and materials of the UN and other international organizations. A single classification provides the basis for a comparative analysis of the colonization of different peoples. DECOLONIAL.IST is open and free for any person or organization. The project builds on the tooling and ecosystem of MITRE ATT&CK. title: Frequently Asked Questions
content: Frequently Asked Questions General The Knowledge Base Classification Who the Project Is For Limitations Origins General What is DECOLONIAL.IST? DECOLONIAL.IST is a knowledge base of Russian colonialism, built on the experience of the peoples who survived it and are living through it still. The project treats the Tsardom of Muscovy, the Russian Empire, the USSR and the Russian Federation as one empire, a single actor of colonial policy. Documented campaigns from the 16th century to the present demonstrate the recurrence of the methods of colonization. Why was DECOLONIAL.IST created? The historical experience of colonized peoples is always fragmented, because colonizers do everything they can to rewrite history in their favor. Archival materials, testimonies, academic research and collective memory exist in scattered form and are rarely considered as parts of a single process. As a result, many events are perceived as isolated historical episodes rather than as manifestations of persistent patterns.DECOLONIAL.IST was created to bring these materials together into a single system – a structured classification that makes it possible to identify recurring mechanisms and to trace the historical continuity of colonial practices.The project demonstrates that the methods of colonial rule used by the Russian state in different historical periods are not a random collection of unrelated events but form a recurring system.DECOLONIAL.IST makes it possible to study these patterns across the last five centuries, to analyze their present-day manifestations, to consider colonial processes as a long-term historical phenomenon, and to compare the practices of Russian colonization with other colonial projects.The project is not only an archive of historical materials but also an instrument of political action. It makes it possible to identify present-day manifestations of (neo)colonial practices, to deconstruct imperial narratives, and to develop systematic approaches to countering them. What is the methodology of DECOLONIAL.IST based on? DECOLONIAL.IST builds on the methodology, structure and tooling of MITRE ATT&CK – the industry standard for studying threats and classifying malicious behaviors in cybersecurity.The approach consists in studying the adversary – namely, its actions: Tactics, Techniques and Procedures. This makes it possible to move from generalities to specifics and to see a system behind scattered historical events.As a result, instead of a list of facts we get a structured catalog of the colonizers' behavior patterns – one we can work with concretely, identify regularities in, and use to build a strategy of resistance. The Knowledge Base What does the knowledge base include? At present, the base contains materials on the methods of colonization the empire has used against: Ukrainians: from 1654 to the present the Nokhchi (Chechens): from 1550 to the presentGoing forward, the project will expand with materials on the peoples of Northern and Eastern Europe, the Caucasus, Central Asia, Siberia, the Arctic and other regions subjected to Russian colonial policy.If you belong to the peoples of these regions, are a historian or a researcher, or simply share the project's goals and want to contribute, we invite you to join the effort, offer your expertise, or provide any other help you can. Classification What is a “tactic”? Tactics reveal the colonizer's motivation, answering the question “what needs to be done right now?” within the overall colonial project. A tactical goal may be, for example, strengthening the colonizer's position in a given territory (the consolidation tactic) or creating the impression that the colonial order is lawful and natural (the legitimization of domination tactic). Techniques are used to achieve tactical goals. What is a “technique”? Techniques answer the question “how?” – they describe the specific methods a colonizer uses to achieve its tactical goals. For example, the aggressor often resorts to the destruction of local knowledge systems and the installation of a new system of governance in order to consolidate its hold on the seized territory. What is a “sub-technique”? A sub-technique is a more specific, lower-level description of the colonizer's action. For example, the aggressor may legislatively ban the native language of an indigenous people in order to consolidate its hold on the seized territory. What is a “procedure”? A procedure is a historical example of a colonizer using a technique or sub-technique in the course of a specific campaign against a specific people. They are listed on the Procedures page and can be filtered by the peoples affected by Russian aggression. What is the difference between a sub-technique and a procedure? Sub-techniques are used to classify actions, while procedures are used to describe how techniques were carried out in real historical events. What is an “actor”? An actor is a historical embodiment of the organizer of colonial conquest – for example, the Russian state in the forms of the Tsardom of Muscovy, the Russian Empire, the USSR and the Russian Federation. What is an “instrument”? An instrument is a specific colonial institution used to achieve the aggressor's tactical goals – for example, the Moscow Patriarchate, the Regular Army or the Secret Police and Security Services. What is a “campaign”? A campaign brings together a specific actor and the instruments and techniques they used against a specific indigenous people in a specific historical period. They are listed on the Campaigns page and can be filtered by the peoples affected by Russian aggression. Who the Project Is For Who can benefit from the project? The project's materials can be used by: researchers and historians; journalists; human rights defenders; activists and decolonial movements; educational initiatives; political and civic organizations. What can the project be used for? The project can be used for: documenting the colonial experience; comparative analysis of historical processes; deconstructing imperial narratives; identifying present-day (neo)colonial practices; developing civic and political strategies of resistance. Limitations How reliable is the information the knowledge base is built on? One of the central problems of colonialism – above all Russian colonialism – is that it strives to rewrite history in its favor, destroying the evidence of its crimes, often together with the witnesses. We rely on a wide range of sources, including historical documents, eyewitness testimonies, the findings of specialist research, and photo and video materials.If you notice information that you believe is incomplete or inaccurate, let us know by emailing contact@decolonial.ist, and we will consider your corrections. How completely are the historical events described? DECOLONIAL.IST is not meant to be a finished or exhaustive system. It is rather an informational foundation – a structure for organizing information that will help the discourse develop further. The project evolves as new research, archival materials and historical testimonies come to light.The materials presented here will be expanded, refined and revised. We claim neither absolute completeness in describing every aspect of Russian colonialism nor complete objectivity. An exhaustive description is impossible – among other reasons because Russian colonialism is, unfortunately, not only history but also the present.Complete objectivity is impossible because all knowledge is situated: it is produced and formulated at a particular historical moment by particular people. We nevertheless strive to cover as many important aspects of Russian colonialism as possible and to present the information in a form that allows it to be verified and examined from different perspectives. We do not hide our position – but we do not impose it on you either. Origins Who developed DECOLONIAL.IST? Since early 2026 the project has been developed by an independent group of decolonial activists, historians and sociologists. It is not affiliated with any organization, party or company and has no external funding.The author of the methodology and curator of the knowledge base is Daniil Yugoslavskiy, a veteran of the Defence Forces of Ukraine, born in Norilsk. Before the 2022 invasion he worked in cybersecurity for ten years and co-authored Atomic Threat Coverage and RE&CT, open knowledge bases built on the MITRE ATT&CK model that underlies DECOLONIAL.IST.

title: Contribute
content: Contribute DECOLONIAL.IST is a non-profit project created by a group of enthusiasts. Below is what we genuinely need help with right now. For any of these, write to contact@decolonial.ist. Chechen translation We need a translator into Chechen (noxçiyn mott): we are preparing a Chechen version of the site, and it cannot be done without a native speaker. If you speak Chechen, or know someone willing to help with the translation, please write to us at contact@decolonial.ist. Books and sources To develop the domain on the colonization of the Nokhchi (Chechens), we need scholarly publications that are hard to obtain. We are currently looking for: M. M. Ibragimov (head of the author team). «История Чечни с древнейших времён до наших дней» (The History of Chechnya from Ancient Times to the Present Day): in 2 volumes. Grozny: GUP "Knizhnoe izdatelstvo", 2006–2008. ISBN 978-5-98896-103-1 (vol. 1), 978-5-98896-101-7 (vol. 2) A. B. Zaks. «Ташев-Хаджи – сподвижник Шамиля» (Tashev-Hadji, an Associate of Shamil). Grozny: Kniga, 1992 A. G. Kavtaradze. «Генерал А. П. Ермолов» (General A. P. Yermolov). Tula: Priokskoe knizhnoe izdatelstvo, 1977 (series «Nashi slavnye zemliaki»). Google Books: 8HPNAAAAMAAJ Zhizn' Natsional'nostei (the Narkomnats periodical). Moscow, 1922, No. 10(139) and No. 16 - Inal Butaev's «Грозненская нефть и Чечня» (Grozny Oil and Chechnya), No. 10, p. 6, and N. Kosterin's «Политическое состояние Горской Республики» (The Political Condition of the Mountain Republic), No. 16, p. 9. Grozny: Groznensky rabochy, 2010. 687 pp. ISBN 978-5-900231-76-1. Grozny, 1988, issues of 16 August and 12 November «Живая память: о жертвах сталинских репрессий» (Living Memory: On the Victims of Stalinist Repressions), compiled by D. Khozhaev. Grozny, 1991 V. Yu. Zorin. «Чечня: кремнистый путь к миру: дневник не для себя» (Chechnya: The Flinty Road to Peace: A Diary Not for Myself). Moscow: Violanta, 1997. 381 pp. ISBN 5-88803-001-5. RSL record: 01001760902 If you have these books in electronic or paper form, or are willing to help us purchase them, please get in touch: contact@decolonial.ist. Expert review We need a professional historian – a specialist in Ukrainian history and Russian colonial policy – to review the Ukrainian domain: fact-checking, wording, and completeness of coverage. Later on, the same kind of review will be needed for the domain on the colonization of the Nokhchi (Chechens), which is currently under development. Our plans include documenting the history of the colonization of other peoples that have suffered from Russian aggression, and we are looking for historians willing to join this work. If you are a historian, or can put us in touch with one, please write to us at contact@decolonial.ist. Financial support We need funds to pay for expert work and IT development. You can support us in any of the following ways: Monobank jar: https://send.monobank.ua/jar/6gfYnkCDso PayPal: paypal@decolonial.ist USDT (TRC-20, TRON): TGdEm7mQC7y3TJ27aFAi5FN9TEijAuApZ5 Bitcoin (BTC): bc1q4jq3arkyk2am7ahw9mzhlx8lkh66hx6ks68t5u Contributors People whose work is part of DECOLONIAL.IST. Contributions to individual techniques, campaigns, actors, and instruments are also credited on the pages of those entries. How you are credited – real name, pseudonym, or anonymously – is your choice; the spelling is agreed with you before publication, including for the site's other languages.
